newsitem.title: USA: Liggett tobacco pact with states expected soon.
newsitem.headline: Liggett tobacco pact with states expected soon.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Liggett Group Inc. and the attorneys general of several states were expected to announce on Thursday a historic settlement of anti-smoking litigation that would contain unprecedented concessions by a tobacco company.
A news conference on the accord was tentatively planned for Thursday afternoon, sources told Reuters, but they cautioned that the deal could still come unravelled.

Anticipation of a possible settlement sent most tobacco stocks plunging. Shares of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the nation's biggest cigarette company, lost $5.625 to $116.375 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most heavily traded issue.
Brooke Group Ltd, which owns Liggett, lost 50 cents to $4.75, also on the NYSE.

Attorneys general involved in the negotiations had been meeting non-stop since Tuesday night to iron out details of the potential settlement with Liggett, which makes Chesterfield and other cigarettes.
"We're hoping for a unanimous deal," Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore, who is spearheading the negotiations with Liggett, told Reuters.

Negotiations between Liggett and the states heated up just after the first anniversary of Liggett's historic break with the industry to become the first cigarette company to offer to settle smoking litigation.

Sources said the potential settlement would include a Liggett offer to turn over potentially damaging documents about the entire industry and would allow current and former employees to testify about Liggett's involvement with other companies.

It would also involve Liggett's agreement to carry a warning label that cigarettes are addictive. This would mark a major break with the rest of the tobacco industry, which has maintained that nicotine is not addictive.
Such a settlement would be the harshest blow yet to the cigarette industry, which is still suffering from two recent court decisions that caused tobacco stocks to tumble.

On Monday the U.S. Supreme Court refused to hear a challenge by Philip Morris Cos. to a Florida law that makes it easier for the state attorney general to recover the costs of treating smoking-related diseases.
Last Thursday the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled that the first suit brought by an attorney general against the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers could proceed to trial in June.

On March 13, 1996, Liggett, which is owned by Bennett LeBow through his Brooke Group, agreed to settle a federal class action in New Orleans. Two days later it reached an accord with five states that sued the industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers. The federal class action has since been thrown out by an appeals court.

Since last year, a total of 22 attorneys general as well as the lieutenant governor of Alabama have filed Medicaid suits against the tobacco industry. Because of this, LeBow has been negotiating a broader agreement that would satisfy a larger number of states.
Pennsylvania, Missouri and Alaska are also considering filing similar suits.

Sources said a key part of the settlement would be LeBow's offer to turn over potentially damaging documents about the entire industry and the prospect that Liggett employees or former employees would testify against other companies.

The expected settlement by Liggett comes amid a U.S. Justice Department criminal investigation into the tobacco industry on several issues, including whether the top officers of the major cigarette makers lied to Congress in 1994 when they testified that nicotine is not addictive.

While the sources were optimistic a settlement would soon be reached to end more state suits against Liggett, they said the larger tobacco companies had made no effort to negotiate directly with the attorneys general or lawyers representing other plaintiffs suing the industry.
They said that if any such industry-wide settlement were to emerge, it would not be for a very long time.
Some states, in particular Minnesota, have previously raised doubts about the proposed Liggett settlement.
